questions.question: Define economics and unpack its elements: needs, wants, the four factors of production with their rewards, and the three basic processes.
questions.expected_answer: Economics is the social science studying how people, businesses and governments use limited resources to satisfy unlimited needs and wants. Needs are survival essentials; wants are desires beyond necessity and renew endlessly. The factors: natural resources (rewarded with rent), labour (wages), capital (interest) and entrepreneurship (profit — the organiser who combines the others and carries risk). The basic processes are production (combining factors to create goods and services), exchange (trading through markets and money) and consumption (using goods to satisfy wants — the chain's end purpose).

questions.question: Distinguish micro from macro with the street test, and positive from normative with an example pair.
questions.expected_answer: Microeconomics studies individual units — one household, one firm, one market ('could you point at it on your street?' — one taxi fare, one shop's price). Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole — inflation, national unemployment, GDP (the drone shot). Positive statements describe what is and can be tested ('petrol rose by ninety cents'); normative statements judge what ought to be ('petrol is too expensive'). Confusing them produces arguments where measurements and wishes talk past each other.

questions.question: Describe the economist's method, the role of ceteris paribus, and why economics is a social science with honest limits.
questions.expected_answer: The loop: observation of real data, hypothesis, testing against statistics and history (the economy cannot be rerun in a lab), and laws/theories that survive — always guarded by ceteris paribus, which isolates one relationship while everything else moves. Tools include data, indices, models (useful simplifications like the circular flow) and graphs. Economics is a social science — its subject is human behaviour — but the most quantitative one, using scientific method. Its limits: people learn and react to predictions, so laws are tendencies, forecasts carry error, and disagreement is normal science, not failure.
